questions.q: Why is table locking duration specifically a code review concern, per this lesson?
options: Some schema changes hold a lock on the entire table for the operation's duration, and on a large, busy table that can cascade into timeouts and a visible outage
SQL Server never locks tables during schema changes, so this is a non-issue
Locking only matters at runtime, never something a reviewer can assess ahead of time
Table locks only occur during SELECT queries, not schema changes
questions.explain: A reviewer needs to assess how long a proposed change will realistically lock a table given its real size and traffic, before it's ever deployed.

questions.q: Why should 'is there a rollback script' be part of code review itself, not an afterthought?
options: It catches a migration that's genuinely hard to reverse before it merges, rather than discovering that under pressure after it's already run in production
Rollback scripts are a legal requirement for all database changes
It has no real benefit; it's purely a formality
SQL Server automatically generates rollback scripts, so this just verifies that feature works
questions.explain: Asking about reversibility during review surfaces genuinely irreversible changes at the safest possible time — before deployment.

questions.q: Beyond helping the query it was written for, what should a reviewer check about a new index?
options: Whether it changes the query optimizer's plan for other, different queries that touch the same table
Whether the index name uses proper casing conventions only
Whether the index was created using SSMS rather than a script
Nothing else — if it helps one query, that's sufficient
questions.explain: An index change can shift the query plan the optimizer picks for other, unrelated queries against the same table, for better or worse.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how does database-specific code review relate to standard app-code review?
options: It's additive — a database change still needs standard review practices, plus locking, rollback, and downstream query impact
It completely replaces standard code review with a different process
It only applies to stored procedures, not to schema changes
It removes the need for readability or naming-convention checks
questions.explain: Database review builds on top of ordinary code review rather than substituting for it.

questions.q: What example did the lesson give of a schema change that can require holding a long lock on a large table?
options: Adding a NOT NULL column with a default value to a large, actively-written table
Running a SELECT query against an indexed view
Renaming a database from within SSMS
Adding a comment to a stored procedure
questions.explain: That kind of change can require validating or writing a default across every existing row, which can be a size-of-table operation depending on version and edition.
